story_text.value:
Huge open source projects have been successful by building upon dozens to hundreds of small libraries that encapsulate functionality and complexity.

AI coding uses these libraries to quickly build applications.

With the latest round of model releases I am seeing that AI can now generate the functionality of almost any library in-line as it generates the application.

When building took a long time, breaking things down into well defined modules, shipping incrementally, and reusing code, were essential techniques. They seem much less important when AI is doing the work.

Is software library creation obsolete?

title.value: Is library building obsoleted by AI coding?

story_text.value:
Switched to Fedora a year ago. And because I needed to transcribe interviews offline from time to time, I was looking for something like MacWhisper for Linux. When I couldn't find one, I decided to build one. Because in this day and age, why the hell not! And yes, AI coding-agents were used.

I work as a .NET Software Engineer and I despise Electron Apps, so I decided to go with a semi-native Stack, consisting of C# and Avalonia.Net (hardware accelerated trough SkiaSharp) for the frontend and C++ for low-level model bindings (CTranslate2 for translation, Nemotron 3 NeMo-Speech.cpp for Speaker Identification via JSON-RPC worker).

A friend liked the app and told me to go Freemium, so here we are. Works also on Windows btw.

title.value: Show HN: TrueScribe – Linux local AI transcription studio

story_text.value:
One topic I've been researching lately is the best way to handle switching to another agent when I hit a usage limit on one of them. For example, if I hit the usage limit on Codex, I would want to switch to Claude Code and vice versa.

The important part is not losing the ongoing context/task(s) when switching between the tools.. I have found a few things that say they do this but none seem to have much traction.

As a result, I was hoping to pick the brain of HN'ers to see how you all handle this

(To head off comments regarding 'pay for a better plan for more usage' - I can't currently really afford the jump from $20 a month per agent to $100-200/m per agent)

title.value: Ask HN: How do you handle hitting AI coding agent usage limits?

story_text.value:
I'm tired of AI coding agents which are good for 30 seconds and then completely fail on the slightest hiccup: a failing test, a temporarily unavailable dependency, an incorrect assumption. Sometimes I end up having to babysit these agents anyway.

Relay is a harness for coding agents which takes advantage of the fact that agents are often good at doing something slightly wrong, and not so good at doing something correctly and completely. Relay repeatedly tries the task and on each failure, uses the output to find a better way to do it.

It does this by running the task in a loop: attempt the task, run the checks in a fresh sandbox, on failure read the error and retry instead, until the checks pass. What it learned from a run is retained, so that it doesn't repeat the same mistake, and when the checks eventually pass, it will ship the change as a normal git PR - no hidden state, no magic, the diff is human readable.

A few specifics:

- it runs locally, is free, and doesn't require an account to run the local agent - it uses a top-tier model to plan/review, and cheaper models to actually write code (for cost reasons) - happy to discuss why this is a good idea and why it isn't - the checks run in an isolated sandbox for each task, rather than "trusting" the agent - currently supports [list actual models/integrations - Opus 5.5, GPT-6, etc] - there's a paid tier for running this unattended across multiple repos with shared sandbox minutes, the actual agent is free.

It's not magic, it's not AGI, and it will fail badly on some problems.

Would appreciate feedback, particularly from people who've deployed agents unattended and found that they don't actually work, or have had to build substantial tooling around them to get useful results.

title.value: Show HN: Relay – a harness for AI coding agents that recover and verify

story_text.value:
TLDR version: ProgressCove, my calm, multiplatform task manager that has a glass half-full perspective, avoids red texts and past due anxiety as it only leads to procrastination.

I talk about: - Brief origin story: How I started writing middleware for another to-do app project status display for Echo Show screen and didn't stop there. - Backend architecture choices: Network segmentation, frameworks and sustainability as a solo dev. - App stack: Expo React Native, WatermelonDB offline first storage with online sync, Cloudflare workers to serve web app, Python FastAPI, PostgreSQL/PgBouncer - AI coding without the slop: How I use Claude as my junior developer under strict technical oversight. - Smart task prioritization: Task and project ordering by a combo metric based on completion percentages, helping users focus on tasks closer to completion and a U-shaped task age decay to surface new items instantly, drop mid-aged tasks, and eventually float old backlog projects. - Smart Home: Home Assistant integration, chores as buttons that dim/highlight based on due status for wall tablets with 10 second debounce window to avoid mistaps. - Soup Mode: Recurring tasks with variations (useful for rotating meals, movies or workout routines) that will randomize your next task. - Advanced options: Keeping things simple and clean for anyone with anxiety and providing secret power user options, such as 8 level deep nesting and ability to name your task tiers, where a project can be a donkey!

Anyone can try out the full-featured, no card required trial for 14 days. All versions, including web app can be found at https://progresscove.com
